title: States and local government
note: Drafted for Prompt 12 (Unit 2). Every lesson is a draft until a person reviews it (content/course/README.md).

listen.explanationKey: Name one power that is only for the federal government.
facts: Some powers are only for the federal government, like printing money and declaring war.
Some powers are only for the states, like schools, police and driver’s licenses.

newWords.meaning: sharing power between the national government and the states

video.title: Federal and State Powers
video.license: Standard YouTube license: shown as a YouTube embed, which YouTube's terms allow; not licensed to Pathways.

story.say: Some powers belong only to the federal government.

help.simpler: Some jobs only the national government can do.
help.example: States cannot print their own money.
help.why: The test asks you to name one power only for the federal government.

story.say: Printing money and declaring war are two of them.

help.simpler: Only the federal government prints money and declares war.
help.example: Every dollar bill comes from the federal government.
help.why: “Print paper money” and “Declare war” are answers on the test.

check.prompt: Tap the powers that only the federal government has.

story.say: Some powers belong only to the states.

help.simpler: Some jobs are done by each state, not by the national government.
help.example: Sharing power between the nation and the states is called federalism.
help.why: The test asks you to name one power only for the states.

story.say: Schools, police and driver’s licenses are run by the states.

help.simpler: States take care of schools, police and driver’s licenses.
help.example: You get your driver’s license from your state, not from the federal government.
help.why: “Give a driver’s license” and “Provide schooling and education” are answers on the test.

check.prompt: Which power belongs to the states?

listen.explanationKey: What is the purpose of the 10th Amendment?
facts: The 10th Amendment says powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or to the people.

newWords.meaning: a change or addition to the Constitution

story.say: The 10th Amendment is one of the first ten amendments: the Bill of Rights.

help.simpler: It is one of the first ten amendments, added in 1791.
help.example: Remember from Unit 1: amendments 1 to 10 are the Bill of Rights.
help.why: Knowing where it comes from helps you remember it.

story.say: It says powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or to the people.

help.simpler: If the Constitution does not give a power to the national government, the states or the people keep it.
help.example: The Constitution does not give schools to the federal government, so the states run them.
help.why: The test asks about the purpose of the 10th Amendment. This is the answer.

check.prompt: What is the purpose of the 10th Amendment?
choices: Powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or the people
It gives every state two senators

story.say: This keeps power shared, not all in one place.

help.simpler: Power is split between the national government and the states.
help.example: Your state makes many rules about daily life, like school and driving rules.
help.why: This sharing is part of the federal system from Unit 1.

check.statement: The 10th Amendment gives all power to the federal government.

readIt.sentence: How many states are in the United States?

listen.explanationKey: What is the capital of your state?
facts: Every state has a capital city and a governor.
The governor leads the state government.
Pathways looks up your state’s capital and governor on an official list, using the state you chose in “Who Represents Me?”.

newWords.meaning: the city where a government meets

story.say: Every state has a capital city and a governor.

help.simpler: Each state has a main city for its government, the capital, and a leader, the governor.
help.example: This is the Colorado State Capitol in Denver, the capital of Colorado.
help.why: The test asks for the capital of your state and the name of your governor.

story.say: The governor leads the state government.

help.simpler: The governor is the top leader of a state.
help.example: A governor is like a President, but for one state.
help.why: The test asks who the governor of your state is now.

story.say: The app looks up your state’s capital and governor on an official list.

help.simpler: The app checks an official list, so the names are right.
help.example: It uses the state you picked in “Who Represents Me?”.
help.why: This way you learn the right answers for your state.

story.say: Here are your state’s capital and governor.

help.simpler: These are the answers for your state.
help.example: Officer: “What is the capital of your state?” You say the capital shown here.
help.why: The test asks for your state’s capital and governor. The answers depend on where you live.

story.say: Check the names again before your interview.

help.simpler: Governors can change after elections. Check again close to your interview.
help.example: If there was an election, a name may be different.
help.why: You want to give the governor serving on your interview day.
